cells.tense: You're here right now with the pen, and the direction is yours to write.
cells.ask: Offer one small start to two people today — say plainly it might not work and you want their read, not their yes; then send the rough version.
cells.core:
You move in unclear situations by starting things on a spark of direction, before you can see the whole road. That bit of fire is enough to get you into the next step, and you trust whatever the next step reveals. Right now that's not a problem you're managing. It's just how you work, and it's working.

The edge is that the spark is stronger than the road. You can light a project, pull a few people toward it, and then stand in the gap where the plan should be — wondering if the light will hold. It does, as long as you don't force the whole path into view before you take the first step. Start the smaller version this week. Let it be unfinished for a while. The direction gets clearer by moving, not by waiting.
cells.sheetLine: You start on a spark, and the next step is enough.
cells.verb: starting things on a spark of direction before the whole road is visible
cells.place: where there is only enough light to take the next step, never enough to see the whole road

cells.tense: You're straining toward a future you can't write in yet, bracing for a road that hasn't shown itself.
cells.ask: Say a plain sentence about the uncertain part and let it stay unanswered today — no pitch, no plan, no fixing.
cells.core:
You're pushing the spark ahead of the road. A direction shows up, barely formed, and before it has time to prove itself you're bracing for a future you can't see yet — explaining it, defending it, trying to land the whole plan in one conversation. The enthusiasm is real, but it's running ahead of what's actually happened.

The push costs you the thing it was for. When you insist on the full road now, the uncertainty that could have revealed something feels like a threat instead of information. You get louder and less convincing, and the people you're pulling toward the project start to feel handled.

Let one uncertain step stay uncertain today. Say what you don't know out loud, in plain words, and then stop explaining. The direction can survive a day of not being defended. In fact that's the only way it grows.

cells.tense: You're still standing at a door that's already behind you, waiting for a direction that was supposed to arrive by now.
cells.ask: Pick one small, ordinary thing you've been circling and do the first ten minutes of it, badly, before you feel ready.
cells.core:
The spark isn't lighting, so you don't start. You circle the thing instead. You read about it, think it through, wait until the picture is clear enough to move. That waiting has started to look like good judgment. It isn't.

The move back is small and unglamorous: ten minutes on something you keep not starting, done badly, before you feel ready. The fire follows the first move. It doesn't precede it. One clumsy step, and the next one gets easier to see.

Nothing here needs conviction first. The clarity you're waiting for is on the other side of the move, not in front of it.

cells.tense: You're at the wheel without your hands on it, writing the direction and calling it the weather.
cells.ask: Take one thing you've described as the situation's fault and say out loud, once, that you chose it. Say it without defending it.
cells.core:
This is happening. When the room is ambiguous and no one knows what to do, you start something, say the confident thing, pull people along. You are the direction more often than you notice. Yet it gets described as if the energy were coming from the project, the moment, the team — as if you just happened to be standing there when the spark arrived.

The steering is running; the ownership isn't. Part of that is a kind of courtesy: not wanting to take credit, not wanting to make it about you. But the people following need to know the direction has a source they can talk to. And you need the same thing. When you don't own it, you also can't adjust it — you're steering a car you're pretending you're not driving.

Start with one thing you've described as the situation. Say it's yours. Not a big speech — just the plain sentence, once. That's how the hand comes back on the wheel.

attempts.check: The record supports that the person is doing this card's work, but not the claim in my Too Much draft that they are trying to inspire people into a particular deadline outcome; the reader could object that no one has asked for that, or that they aren't converting anything. The similar overreach is in the Too Little draft's 'you used to be able to say it' — the record only says the seat is starved, not that a confident public voice existed before. The asks survive being wrong because each is a small behavioral move that teaches the person something even if my read is off; the only sentence that serves me more than them is the Too Much core's 'You're selling a future to people who never asked for one,' so I've made it specific to the push, not to a motive.
